job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many students believe that only living things or moving objects qualify as resources, while inanimate items like rocks are useless. However, in geography, a resource is anything that satisfies human needs, regardless of whether it is alive or stationary. Rocks, for instance, are vital natural resources used in construction and manufacturing. Another common misunderstanding is that renewable resources, like solar energy or water, are infinite and can never be exhausted. While these replenish naturally, their availability depends on careful management; over-extraction can lead to scarcity. Furthermore, some people argue that human-made resources, such as bridges or technology, are not 'real' resources compared to natural ones. In reality, human-made resources are essential because humans use their knowledge and skills to transform natural materials into more valuable forms. Finally, we must address the belief that land degradation is solely the result of natural disasters like floods. While nature plays a role, human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and excessive use of chemical fertilizers are the primary drivers of land degradation today. Sustainable development requires us to manage all these resources wisely to ensure they remain available for future generations.

items.evidence: However, in geography, a resource is anything that satisfies human needs, regardless of whether it is alive or stationary.
items.q: A stone lies still and is not alive. What decides whether it counts as a resource?
options: Whether it meets some human need
Whether it is alive and growing
Whether it can move from place to place
Whether humans have changed its form
items.explain: A resource is anything that satisfies human needs, whether it is alive or not, moving or still.

wrong.why: thinks only living things are resources
confuses being a resource with how it is classified by origin

items.evidence: While these replenish naturally, their availability depends on careful management; over-extraction can lead to scarcity.
items.q: A town pumps out far more groundwater than rain refills each year. What will happen?
options: Its water can become scarce over time
Its water will never run out at all
Its water is gone forever, never returning
Its water runs short only in drought years
items.explain: Renewable resources refill naturally, but over-extraction without careful management can still cause scarcity.

wrong.why: thinks renewable resources never run out
thinks used water can never come back
thinks only nature, not overuse, causes shortage

items.evidence: In reality, human-made resources are essential because humans use their knowledge and skills to transform natural materials into more valuable forms.
items.q: Why is a bridge counted as a real and important resource?
options: Because skill turned raw materials into something more useful
Because only the natural rocks inside it count
Because it carries moving people and vehicles
Because it lasts forever without any care
items.explain: Humans use knowledge and skill to change natural materials into more valuable forms, like bridges.

wrong.why: thinks human-made resources are not real resources
picks durability instead of value added by skill

items.evidence: While nature plays a role, human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and excessive use of chemical fertilizers are the primary drivers of land degradation today.
items.q: A village has had no floods for years, but its land is degrading. What is most likely to blame?
options: Tree cutting, overgrazing and heavy fertilizer use
Heavy rains and other natural events alone
Too little fertilizer put on the fields
Fields left unused to conserve the soil
items.explain: Human activities like deforestation, overgrazing and too much chemical fertilizer are the main causes of land degradation today.

wrong.why: thinks only natural events degrade land
thinks conservation means leaving land untouched
